newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan open hotline with goodwill chat.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan open hotline with goodwill chat.

text.p: In a symbolic gesture of mutual goodwill, the prime ministers of India and Pakistan on Thursday spoke for the first time on a telephone "hotline" set up to help dispel mistrust between the two longtime foes.

Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, held a brief conversation to initiate the direct line between their offices, and the Indian leader predicted the link would help them "feel better".
"How are you feeling?" Gujral asked Sharif in Urdu during the chat, filmed by Reuters Television.
"It's a very good thing that we have established this."
The two leaders spoke ahead of a fresh round of peace talks set to start later on Thursday in Islamabad between the two nations' highest ranking career diplomats.
Gujral and Sharif had agreed to set up the direct phone link between their two offices when they met for the first time in the Maldives last month on the sidelines of a regional summit.
They were the highest level bilateral talks between the two nations in four years.

"The good thing is that the foreign secretaries are talking. This telephone line is also established. We can often talk to each other on phone. We'll feel better," the Indian leader, who spoke a mixture of Urdu and English, told Sharif.
Pakistani Foreign Secretary Shamshad Ahmed and his Indian counterpart, Salman Haider, were scheduled to begin five days of talks later on Thursday.
The two senior diplomats met in New Delhi in March to restart bilateral talks which had become bogged down in 1994 in disagreement over Kashmir.
Both India and Pakistan stake a claim over the divided Himalayan region, and two of the three wars they have fought since independence in 1947 have been caused by their dispute over Kashmir.
